specAnchors.text: understand, in terms of intermolecular forces, physical properties shown by substances, including: i the trends in boiling temperatures of alkanes with increasing chain length ii the effect of branching in the carbon chain on the boiling temperatures of alkanes iii the relatively low volatility (higher boiling temperatures) of alcohols compared to alkanes with a similar number of electrons iv the trends in boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides HF to HI

primer.text: Boiling point is a tally of intermolecular strength, so three levers move it: how much surface a molecule exposes, how many electrons it carries, and whether it can hydrogen bond. This note applies each lever to alkanes, alcohols and the hydrogen halides, and shows why HF breaks the trend line its own group follows.

modules.title: Chain shape and electron count
modules.opening: Two levers control the London contribution to boiling point: how much of the molecule touches its neighbours, and how many electrons it drags around. This lesson works both, comparing branched against straight chains and reading the noble-gas and alkane graphs.
keyPoints: Larger molecular surface area means more contact with adjacent molecules and stronger induced attractions.
Branching reduces surface area, weakening London forces and lowering boiling points.
More electrons raise the chance and size of temporary dipoles, strengthening induced forces.
Boiling points of the noble gases climb as electron counts grow.
The alkane graph shows the same climb: longer chains boil higher.

low.restatement: A stretched chain touches many neighbours and its many electrons flicker strongly, so it boils high; a branched or small-electron molecule touches less and boils lower.
low.analogy: A long plank lying flat touches the whole shelf beneath it, while a crumpled ball of the same wood touches only at a few points - plank chains stick, ball chains roll apart.
low.examPointer: For isomer comparisons, hold the electron count equal and argue only through surface area - mixing the two levers loses the comparison mark.

medium.restatement: Contact area scales the induced-dipole interaction, so branching lowers it at fixed formula; electron count sets both the frequency and magnitude of instantaneous dipoles, which is why the noble-gas series climbs monotonically.
medium.analogy: A wide paintbrush covers a wall in one stroke (large contact, strong grip) while a slim brush needs many passes; heavier pigment (more electrons) makes every stroke grip harder.
medium.examPointer: Quote both graphs' message in one line: boiling point rises with electron count and falls with branching - then name the force responsible, London dispersion.

modules.title: Why alcohols outboil their alkanes
modules.opening: Swap one CH2 for an OH and the boiling point leaps tens of degrees. This lesson traces the jump to hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules, against the mere induced pulls their alkane cousins manage.
keyPoints: Alcohols carry O-H bonds, so their molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
The oxygen pulls the shared electrons away, leaving each hydrogen delta-positive.
Those hydrogens reach lone pairs on neighbouring oxygens, forming hydrogen bonds.
Alkanes manage only induced dipole-dipole forces between their molecules.
Propane boils at -42 degrees while propanol reaches 97 degrees.

low.restatement: The O-H group lets alcohol molecules hook together strongly; alkane molecules only nudge each other, so separating alcohols takes far more energy.
low.analogy: Alcohol molecules shake hands firmly across the gap; alkane molecules brush sleeves. Undoing handshakes costs more effort than brushing sleeves apart.
low.examPointer: Name both the force in the alcohol (hydrogen bonding) and the force in the alkane (induced dipole-dipole) - naming only one loses the comparison mark.

medium.restatement: Electronegative oxygen polarises the O-H bond, giving hydrogen enough positive character to bond a lone pair on the next molecule's oxygen; the alkane's C-H bonds stay essentially non-polar, so induced forces remain its only intermolecular resource.
medium.analogy: One molecule carries a key ring (delta-positive hydrogens) and the next carries the locks (lone pairs); the alkane has neither keys nor locks and relies on leaning against its neighbour.
medium.examPointer: Quote the propane/propanol figures when asked for evidence - the 139-degree spread is the numbers behind the mechanism.

modules.title: The hydrogen halides and their outlier
modules.opening: From HCl to HI the boiling points climb smoothly as electrons accumulate - but HF breaks the pattern, boiling hundreds of degrees above its slot. This lesson assigns each force its share of the credit.
keyPoints: The hydrogen halides' boiling points rise from HCl through HBr to HI.
Larger halogens carry more electrons, so induced dipole-dipole forces strengthen along the series.
HF sits far above the trend because its molecules hydrogen bond.
The H-F bond is highly polar, leaving hydrogen strongly positive.
Fluorine's small, intense lone pairs complete the hydrogen-bond link between neighbours.

low.restatement: Down the halogen group the molecules fatten with electrons, so induced forces and boiling points rise together; HF jumps off the line because only it can hydrogen bond.
low.analogy: Three siblings grow steadily heavier with age (HCl, HBr, HI), but the youngest (HF) carries a backpack no sibling has - the hydrogen-bond kit - and outweighs them all.
low.examPointer: Sketch the graph with HF plotted as a high outlier above the HCl-HI line, then label the outlier 'hydrogen bonding'.

medium.restatement: Electron count drives the induced contribution from chlorine to iodine; in HF the bond polarity concentrates charge at hydrogen and fluorine's compact lone pairs accept a link, adding an entirely new force channel that dominates the boiling point.
medium.analogy: The series adds passengers one by one (electrons), but HF also bolted on a tow bar (hydrogen bonding) that hauls its boiling point clear of the queue.
medium.examPointer: Say 'hydrogen bonds between HF molecules' explicitly - 'polarity alone' explanations fail because HCl is also polar yet sits on the trend line.

glossary.definition: The induced dipole-dipole attraction whose strength scales with electron count and molecular contact area.
A skeletal rearrangement that shrinks molecular surface area and so weakens induced attractions between isomers.
The boiling-point excess a substance shows above its trend line because its molecules hydrogen bond.
